extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers, graduate students, and practitioners in advertising/marketing research (and grant reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply methodological, measurement, and substantive criteria used to design, evaluate, and interpret empirical research in advertising, marketing communications, and consumer behavior. Emphasizes experimental and field methods, measurement instruments, statistical testing, and practical implications for advertising strategy and policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-controlled experimental methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: The computer-controlled experimental methodology is an efficient and reliable means to study marketing communications and buyer behavior; it offers capacity to monitor response times in units of one ten-thousandth of a second by using the computer clock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages include fine-grained timing measurement and the ability to test response processes; used to develop buyer behavior models with empirical support. Example application: simultaneous concept testing with computer-controlled experiments. Use when precise temporal measurement of responses is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response time as unobtrusive measure of message favorability
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings suggest rapidity of response is related to favorability of message content: favorable messages processed most rapidly and neutral messages least rapidly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret response latency as an indicator of favorability; useful as an unobtrusive measure for analysis and evaluation of message content. Consider validity threats (e.g., motor speed differences) and complement with other measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empathic skills measurement for advertising communicators (Type I and Type II tests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional communicators tested for two types of empathic skill: sensitivity to individual differences (Type I; Guilford tests) and sensitivity to the generalized other (Type II; Judgment of Interests test). Hypothesis: professional advertising communicators will be more empathic than the population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established psychometric instruments (Guilford, Johnson's JI), compare means to normative/population data, and perform statistical significance tests (reported .001 and .05 levels in examples). Ensure testing under proper supervision and appropriate comparison groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of normative data and assumption-checking (normality)
rubrics_metrics.description: When using Guilford test norms, assume social acuity is normally distributed and use Guilford test means and standard deviations as population parameters; check assumptions (e.g., normality) with experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document and justify any assumptions about population distribution; consult domain experts (example: Dr. Nancy Wiggins approved the normality assumption). If data deviate from normality, apply appropriate scaling or transformation methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of effects as advertising goals/criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising goals can be defined as stages in a 'hierarchy of effects': belief/knowledge stage, attitude/feeling stage, behavioral intention stage, and action/purchase stage. Each stage should be meaningfully related to subsequent stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these stages as criteria for monitoring advertising effect; design measures to capture each stage and test sequential relationships (e.g., via longitudinal data). Consider that consumer behavior is purposeful and stages should logically influence later stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longitudinal panel data to test sequential advertising effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Use longitudinal panels (e.g., MRCA panel of 182 housewives) to observe consumers over time and under natural conditions to test sequential assumptions implicit in hierarchy-of-effects models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longitudinal measurement provides insight into causal order and temporal dynamics; use panels to examine prediction of purchase from prior attitudes and other predictors. Ensure panel representativeness and account for attrition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fishbein attitude measurement (expectancy × value summation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure attitude by multiplying the likelihood a belief is true (expectancy) by the evaluation of the belief's attribute (value) for each belief statement, then summing across beliefs to represent attitude toward the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fishbein measure is a significant predictor of subsequent purchase but may not outperform other commonly used predictors. Investigate moderators (e.g., involvement, confidence) that limit attitude-behavior relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderators of attitude-behavior relationship (involvement and confidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Involvement with the product and confidence in one's ability to judge the product were found to be important moderators of the relationship between summated attitude measures and actual purchase behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating attitude-based predictions, measure and test potential moderators; do not assume attitude alone fully determines behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cluster analysis for segmenting consumers by purchase sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Use cluster analysis on panel/purchase-sequence data to segment consumers into groups based on product purchase sequences, then characterize segments by demographic and socioeconomic profiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segments defined this way can reveal meaningful market structure and guide strategy. Apply across product classes cautiously; expect different segment patterns for different product types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validation and reliability testing of measurement instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Developed measuring instruments (e.g., for personality, product perception) should be subjected to validity and reliability testing before use in field studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate instrument psychometrics (construct validity, reliability) and document testing procedures and results. Use validated scales to support typologies and subsequent analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of AID and MCA (computer techniques) to identify interacting explanatory variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine Automatic Interaction Detector (AID) and Multiple Classification Analysis (MCA) to empirically determine which variables and combinations best distinguish individuals with different levels of information-seeking behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these techniques to detect interactions and construct complex explanatory variables (e.g., 'lifestyle'). Use tandem methods to assess both separate and combined effects; ensure appropriate sample size and interpretability of interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study interaction between message-bound and audience-bound factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Research should analyze how message-bound factors (e.g., price information, persuasive appeal) interact with audience-bound factors (e.g., needs, values, experience) in affecting communications response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments or field studies to test cross-factor interactions; avoid assuming additive effects. Example: price communicates quality more strongly under high perceived purchase risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing transferability of advertising strategies across national markets (Lens Judgment Model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a Lens Judgment Model (decision-maker selects and weights environmental cues) and combine quantitative data with case-study interviews to predict likelihood that creative/media strategies will transfer successfully from one national market to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine cross-sectional quantitative analyses with qualitative interviews of executives to capture decision criteria; use model to predict transfer success but validate with field evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical modeling of advertising effect and budget optimization
rubrics_metrics.description: Critically evaluate existing mathematical models for advertising effect and methods to determine optimum advertising budget; empirical testing requires sufficient firm data to estimate parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperate with firms to obtain real-world data; recognize that data insufficiency can prevent parameter estimation or adequate validity testing. Apply models cautiously and report limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of field-test analogies for public policy evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose resolving public policy questions (e.g., unit pricing) by 'test marketing' public policy via field tests evaluated in terms of social benefit criteria, analogous to product test marketing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design policy field experiments and evaluate outcomes on social benefit metrics; consider differing stakeholder perspectives (advertisers vs government officials) when interpreting results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segment-specific appeals versus general appeals — cost-benefit caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimentally compare segment-specific appeals to general appeals; evidence here showed individuals tended to read their own values into general appeals, suggesting additional expense of multiple segment-specific appeals may not be justifiable for some product categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overgeneralizing results beyond studied product categories; test cost-effectiveness by product and audience before committing to segment-specific creative strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure effects of perceived risk, self-confidence, and tangible cues on price-quality inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Price's influence on perceptions of quality is strongest when perceived purchase risk is high, self-confidence is low, and tangible cues for judging product are absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting price-quality signaling, include measures of perceived risk, consumer confidence, and presence of tangible quality cues; tailor pricing communications accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical implications should guide advertising strategy (timing and content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings on information-seeking behavior (e.g., rapid turnover of prospective purchasers) imply advertising practitioners should adjust timing and content of advertising to match consumer decision timeframes and prior experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical findings on decision time and information search to schedule and craft messages; consider prior exposure and learning effects that limit subsequent search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling and sample-size transparency and representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Report and use appropriate sample sizes and samples (e.g., national random sample of 1,300 households; 464 professional communicators across agencies) to support generalizability claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document sampling frames, inclusion/exclusion (e.g., exclusion of Alaska), and sub-sample sizes for subgroup analyses. Acknowledge limits to generalizability from specific samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary comparison of practitioner and researcher perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that academic researchers focus on widely generalizable models while practitioners focus on specific applications; research should explore ways the two disciplines might interact meaningfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame research questions and dissemination to address both general theoretical insight and practitioner-applicable recommendations; consider practitioner input in study design for applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop consumer-product-marketing typologies tied to behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Create typologies linking consumer personality, product characteristics (e.g., conspicuousness, relatedness), and marketing activities to facilitate segmentation and strategy decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build typologies using validated measures and field data; use them to tailor creative and media strategies and to differentiate brand behavioral patterns from competitors.
